title: How rockets reach orbit
examples: How does gravity keep satellites up there?
What is the right speed to stay in orbit?
Is it like throwing a ball really hard?

explain.say: Today we learn how rockets reach orbit around Earth. Gravity is a force that pulls everything toward Earth. This pull is what keeps us on the ground.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: the stages of a rocket. Look at the escape tower, the crew capsule and the third stage. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
An orbit is actually like falling around the Earth. You are constantly falling, but you are also moving sideways. This keeps you going around.
To stay in orbit, you need a very high speed. This speed is what counters the pull of gravity. It keeps you from falling straight down.
A rocket must reach a certain speed and height. This combination allows it to enter a stable orbit. This is much faster than anything we can do on the ground.
Think about throwing a baseball really hard into the air. It goes up, slows down, and falls back down. To orbit, you need that initial push to be much, much greater.
In real life, the International Space Station orbits Earth. It moves very fast while constantly falling around our planet. This shows us orbit in action.

faq.q: Why don't satellites fall down to Earth?
faq.a: Satellites are moving sideways so fast that as gravity pulls them down, they also curve around the Earth. This keeps them in a continuous fall around the planet.
asks: Does gravity pull them down all the time?

faq.q: Is speed the only thing that matters for orbit?
faq.a: No, you need both the right speed and the correct altitude. The speed must be high enough to balance the pull of Earth's gravity at that height.
asks: Do I need to be high up too?
What if I go too slow?

faq.q: Is it like throwing a ball really hard?
faq.a: It is similar, but much more extreme. Throwing a ball only gets you so far; an orbiting object needs a constant, high horizontal velocity.
asks: Does the initial push matter a lot?

faq.q: What is the difference between falling and orbiting?
faq.a: Falling suggests stopping or hitting something. Orbiting means continuously falling around a body without ever hitting it, due to high sideways speed.
asks: What is the difference between the two?

faq.q: Does the Earth's gravity change with distance?
faq.a: Yes, gravity weakens as you move farther away from the center of the Earth. This changes what speed you need to maintain a stable orbit.
asks: Does gravity get weaker up high?
Does the pull change with altitude?

facts: Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward the center of mass.
An orbit is a curved path around a star or planet.
To achieve orbit, an object must reach a specific high horizontal speed.
The International Space Station orbits Earth at a high speed.

quiz.say: If a rocket slows down while in orbit, what will happen?

options.show: It will shoot away from Earth.
options.say: It will shoot away from Earth.

options.show: It will change its orbit shape.
options.say: It will change its orbit shape.

options.show: It will fall closer to Earth.
options.say: It will fall closer to Earth.

quiz.why: Slowing down means the sideways speed is reduced, allowing gravity to pull the object inward.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the force of gravity always pulls toward the center of the Earth.
wrong.1: While the shape changes, the primary effect of losing speed is falling inward, not just changing the curve.
wrong.3: This is wrong because gravity is still pulling, so it cannot stop moving.

quiz.say: What is necessary to keep an object in orbit around Earth?

options.show: Being very close to Earth's surface.
options.say: Being very close to Earth's surface.

quiz.why: The high speed provides the necessary momentum to continuously 'miss' the Earth while falling.

wrong.0: Engines are used to get there, but the orbit itself is maintained by speed and gravity.
wrong.1: Constant upward thrust would keep it away from Earth, not in orbit around it.
wrong.2: Being too close means the speed is not high enough to overcome the strong pull of gravity.

quiz.say: Which statement best describes an orbit?

options.show: A path that only works at the surface.
options.say: A path that only works at the surface.

options.show: A continuous state of falling around a planet.
options.say: A continuous state of falling around a planet.

options.show: A straight line path away from Earth.
options.say: A straight line path away from Earth.

options.show: A path that requires no speed at all.
options.say: A path that requires no speed at all.

quiz.why: This definition captures the balance between the pull of gravity and the object's forward motion.

wrong.0: Orbits happen at various altitudes, not just at ground level.
wrong.2: This describes escaping Earth's gravity, not staying in orbit.
wrong.3: No speed means the object would simply fall straight down due to gravity.
